title: What a Diff'rence a Day Makes

meta.title: Who originally recorded "What a Diff'rence a Day Makes"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Dinah Washington's 1959 hit was a cover. Maria Grever wrote the song in 1934 as "Cuando vuelva a tu lado", and the earliest recording anyone can date is the Dorsey Brothers' Decca side of 29 October 1934.
meta.ogTitle: Who originally recorded 'What a Diff'rence a Day Makes'?
meta.ogDescription: Not a 1959 original: the song is Maria Grever's 1934 "Cuando vuelva a tu lado", and it was on two labels in two languages before Dinah Washington turned eleven.

answer.label: Not a Dinah Washington original — and not the Spanish record usually named in her place
answer.originalArtistDates: Active 1934–1935 · American dance band led by Tommy and Jimmy Dorsey, recording for Decca in New York
answer.sourceLine: Dinah Washington’s 1959 Mercury single is so completely hers that the song is routinely treated as starting there. It does not: María Grever wrote it in 1934 as the Spanish song “Cuando vuelva a tu lado,” and Stanley Adams supplied the English lyric the same year. The usual correction — that Orquesta Pedro Vía recorded it first — is where our research parts company with the reference books: Vía’s Victor master was cut in New York on 10 December 1934, six weeks after the Dorsey Brothers’ Orchestra, with Bob Crosby singing, had already put the English version on wax for Decca on 29 October 1934. The Dorsey side is the earliest recording of the song we can date to a day; Vía’s is the earliest we can date in Spanish. A 1934 English record by the Cleveland singer Jimmie Ague is reported to be earlier still, but no source we found gives it a date.

original.heading: Who recorded it first
original.label: Decca
original.released: Recorded in New York on 29 October 1934 (matrix 38914) and issued the same year as a 10-inch Decca 78, catalogue number 283, under the English title “What a Diff’rence a Day Made,” with a vocal chorus by Bob Crosby.
original.charted: A genuine hit: it reached number 5 in the American listings in the autumn of 1934 — the most successful of the song’s early records, and still forgotten within a generation.
original.cover: Dinah Washington’s 1959 Mercury single reached number 8 on the Billboard Hot 100 and number 4 R&B, won the Grammy for Best Rhythm and Blues Performance and entered the Grammy Hall of Fame in 1998.

trail: The Internet Archive’s catalogue record for the digitised Decca 283 A ↗ dates the Dorsey Brothers’ English recording, with Bob Crosby singing, to 29 October 1934, matrix 38914.

UCSB’s Discography of American Historical Recordings ↗ reconstructs the Spanish session from Victor’s blue history card and ledgers: 10 December 1934, Studio 2, New York, with Pedro Vía on trumpet and leading, a vocalist logged as Chiquito, and Alfredo Cibelli directing — six weeks after the Decca date.
MusicBrainz ↗ holds the composition as a Spanish-language work credited to María Grever as both composer and lyricist, ISWC T-070.028.704-2.

authors.name: Dorsey Brothers’ Orchestra
authors.heading: Dorsey Brothers’ Orchestra
authors.metaLine: Active 1934–1935 · American dance band led by Tommy and Jimmy Dorsey, recording for Decca
authors.bio: Tommy and Jimmy Dorsey had worked together as a studio unit since the late 1920s; in 1934 they put a permanent touring band on the road and signed to the newly founded Decca label. On 29 October 1934, in New York, the band recorded Stanley Adams’s English version of Grever’s song with a vocal chorus by Bob Crosby — matrix 38914, issued on Decca 283. It reached number 5 in the American listings that autumn, and it is the earliest recording of the song we can date to a specific day. The brothers fell out and split the band in 1935.

authors.name: Orquesta Pedro Vía
authors.heading: Orquesta Pedro Vía
authors.metaLine: Latin dance orchestra · recorded for Victor in New York, 1934
authors.bio: Pedro Vía led a small Latin dance band — violin, bass, trumpet, guitar, two pianos and traps — that cut sides for Victor in New York in 1934. On 10 December that year the group recorded María Grever’s “Cuando vuelva a tu lado” in Victor’s Studio 2, with a male vocal refrain credited on the ledger simply as Chiquito and Alfredo Cibelli directing the date. The master, BS-86425, was issued on the 10-inch Victor 32361. It is the earliest recording of the song in Spanish that we could document, and the record most reference works name as the first — but the Decca side had reached the studio six weeks earlier.

authors.name: Dinah Washington
authors.heading: Dinah Washington
authors.metaLine: 1924–1963 · American jazz, blues and R&B singer
authors.bio: Born Ruth Lee Jones, Washington was one of the most popular Black women on record in the 1950s and called herself the Queen of the Blues. Her 1959 Mercury version of the song was her first top-ten pop hit, reaching number 8 on the Billboard Hot 100, and it won the Grammy for Best Rhythm and Blues Performance; it entered the Grammy Hall of Fame in 1998. The reading is definitive enough that most listeners assume she introduced the song. The only error in that assumption is chronological.

authors.name: María Grever
authors.heading: María Grever
authors.bio: Grever was the first Mexican woman composer to win an international audience, and this is the song she is remembered for. She wrote both words and music of “Cuando vuelva a tu lado” in 1934; MusicBrainz credits her as composer and lyricist of the work, and Victor’s own ledgers name her on both counts. The English lyric that carried the song into the American songbook was written separately by Stanley Adams (1907–1994), later the long-serving president of ASCAP. Grever died in 1951, eight years before the recording that made the song famous.

misattribution.heading: What’s actually true
misattribution.intro: This one has two errors stacked on top of each other — the popular one, and a second one inside the usual correction.

items.who: Dinah Washington originated the song in 1959
items.why: Her Mercury single is a cover. The song was written and recorded in 1934, and Washington was born in 1924.

items.who: María Grever, with English lyrics by Stanley Adams
items.why: Victor’s ledgers and MusicBrainz both credit Grever as composer and lyricist of the Spanish original; Adams wrote the English lyric, published late in 1934.

items.who: Orquesta Pedro Vía recorded it first, in 1934
items.why: Vía’s Victor master was cut on 10 December 1934. The Dorsey Brothers’ Decca side with Bob Crosby is dated 29 October 1934 — six weeks earlier. Vía’s is the earliest recording in Spanish, not the earliest recording.

items.who: Dorsey Brothers’ Orchestra, Decca 283 A, 29 October 1934
items.why: It is the earliest recording of the song carrying a date we could confirm against a discographical source.

items.who: Jimmie Ague recorded the English version before the Dorsey Brothers
items.why: Wikipedia and songswithearlierhistories.com both name a 1934 record by the Cleveland singer Jimmie Ague, and another by Freddy Martin’s orchestra the same year, but neither source gives a session or release date. If one turns up earlier than 29 October, this answer changes.

misattribution.truthLine: Washington did not originate it — and on the dates we can verify, neither did the Spanish record usually named in her place.

context.heading: Why the 1959 record swallowed the 1934 ones
lead: The song had a busy 1934 and almost nobody remembers it. Grever wrote it in Spanish, Stanley Adams put an English lyric on it and it was published late that year, and within months there were competing records on two labels in two languages — a Decca side by the Dorsey Brothers with a young Bob Crosby singing in October, a Victor side by Orquesta Pedro Vía in December, and, reportedly, English versions by the Cleveland singer Jimmie Ague and by Freddy Martin’s orchestra that nobody has managed to date. None of them became the song’s permanent address.

Twenty-five years is a long time for a standard to sit around waiting, and what Washington did with it in 1959 was less a cover than a repossession. The Mercury record won a Grammy, put her in the pop top ten for the first time, and fixed a tempo and a mood that every later version answers to. Once a song has a definitive performance, its earlier life stops being audible — which is how a Mexican composer’s 1934 song ends up filed under American R&B.
detailsBody: 1934 — María Grever writes “Cuando vuelva a tu lado” in Spanish.
1934 — Stanley Adams writes the English lyric; the song is published late in the year under the title “What a Diff’rence a Day Made.”
1934 — English recordings by Jimmie Ague and by Freddy Martin’s orchestra are reported this year; no source we found dates either one.
29 October 1934 — the Dorsey Brothers’ Orchestra records the English version with a vocal chorus by Bob Crosby; issued on Decca 283 A, matrix 38914. It reaches number 5.
10 December 1934 — Orquesta Pedro Vía records the Spanish original in Victor’s New York Studio 2, matrix BS-86425, issued on Victor 32361.
1959 — Dinah Washington records it for Mercury; the single reaches number 8 on the Billboard Hot 100 and wins a Grammy for Best Rhythm and Blues Performance.
1998 — Washington’s recording is inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame.
context.pull: The song was already on two labels in two languages when Washington was ten years old.

schema.faqAnswer: No. The song is María Grever's 1934 Spanish song "Cuando vuelva a tu lado", with an English lyric by Stanley Adams; the earliest recording anyone has dated is the Dorsey Brothers' Orchestra, with a vocal chorus by Bob Crosby, cut for Decca in New York on 29 October 1934. Orquesta Pedro Vía's Spanish recording followed on 10 December 1934, and Dinah Washington's 1959 Mercury single is a cover.
